strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing multimodal benchmarks and geometry-focused datasets (GeoQA, Geometry3K, MathVerse, etc.) emphasize higher-order mathematical reasoning rather than Bearer [REDACTED] perception, and GePBench targets this foundational skill explicitly.

The benchmark is substantial and well-constructed: a documented synthesis pipeline (Algorithm 1), 80K figures and 285K questions spanning six aspects (existence, counting, location, size, reference, relationship), easy/hard splits, and deliberate noise injection to simulate degraded visual conditions.

Evaluation breadth is impressive: 20 closed- and open-source MLLMs with matched zero-shot protocols (temperature 0, uniform resolution, validated answer parsing with 99.9% manual verification), plus a human baseline (99.3% accuracy) that establishes the tasks are well-posed.

Ablations are informative: the study of visual encoders (Table 2) shows that higher resolution and mixed-encoder configurations degrade spatial accuracy, providing actionable design insight beyond just reporting model scores.

The paper goes beyond diagnosis: training LLaVA-GeP with the synthesis engine and demonstrating transfer gains on downstream benchmarks (with a from-scratch LLaVA-1.5 control trained identically) strengthens the claim that geometric perception is a foundational capability.

Reproducibility considerations are good: model checkpoints and versions are listed, prompts and training hyperparameters are given in appendices, and the authors commit to public release of code and data.
weaknesses: The main claim that GePBench measures genuine geometric perception rather than template artifacts is not fully established. GPT-4o and Claude-3.5 scoring below chance (17.5%/17.9%) on the 'size' aspect is suspicious; below-random performance on synthetic, procedurally generated figures may indicate distractor design or systematic answer-position biases rather than a true perceptual deficiency, and the paper offers no distractor-bias or answer-frequency analysis to rule this out.

Originality is moderate: perceptual probing of MLLMs has been studied in prior work (e.g., BLINK, Cambrian-1/CV-Bench, MMVP/Eyes Wide Shut, VSR-style spatial benchmarks). The paper positions itself against math-reasoning geometry datasets but does not compare against or clearly differentiate from these perception-focused benchmarks, weakening the novelty case.

The domain-gap concern is under-addressed: all figures are Matplotlib-rendered synthetic shapes with limited stylistic variety. The claimed relevance to real-world applications (medical imaging, chart understanding) is asserted but only weakly evidenced by a modest ~2.2% average downstream improvement.

The LLaVA-GeP transfer results are thin: improvements are small and uneven across benchmarks, there is no error analysis of why gains occur on specific subcategories beyond brief qualitative claims, and no comparison against alternative ways to obtain similar gains (e.g., other synthetic perception data).

Some inconsistencies and shallow analyses reduce confidence: Figure 4 references a figure for encoder results that appears to be a table, some ablation findings (e.g., noise sometimes improving performance) are explained only speculatively, and the evaluation uses models from Dec. 2024, which will be dated by ICML 2026.
The 'scaling yields limited improvements' conclusion is drawn from only a few model families (4 pairs) and could be confounded by differing training data recipes rather than scale per se.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and relevant gap: isolating Bearer [REDACTED] perception from higher-order mathematical reasoning, which most geometry benchmarks (GeoQA, Geometry3K, MathVista) conflate with reasoning.
The evaluation breadth is substantial: 20 MLLMs including strong closed-source models (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-1.5-Pro), with detailed per-aspect, easy/hard splits reported in Table 1.

The benchmark construction is systematic and verifiable by construction: structured descriptions -> rendering -> templated QA generation with programmatically guaranteed ground truth, plus a data engine that can also produce training data (Algorithm 1).
Useful ablation analyses are included: effect of number of shapes, visual encoder comparison (Table 2), noise sensitivity (Figure 10), and a cross-benchmark human-vs-model gap analysis (Figure 7).
Human evaluation, answer-parsing validation (99.9% extraction accuracy), and model checkpoint details in the appendix improve reproducibility of the evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: Evidence of a possible artifact problem that is not adequately investigated: GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet score 17.5% and 17.9% on easy 'size' questions, well below the 25% random-guessing floor. Below-random performance on the *easy* split is a red flag for systematic distractor biases or answer-option ordering artifacts rather than (or in addition to) genuine perceptual failure. The paper offers no text-only or answer-prior ablation to rule out that models exploit option statistics rather than perception.

Distractor and question quality is under-validated. For example, in Figure 1 the 'reference' question asks which shape is smaller than the circle, and it is unclear whether the answer is unique among four candidates. The human study involves only 5 undergraduates on small subsets; no distractor-ambiguity audit or larger human calibration is provided.

The central downstream claim ('substantial improvements') is overstated: the average gain of LLaVA-GeP over LLaVA-1.5 is only 2.2% across math/chart benchmarks, with mixed or negligible changes on general benchmarks (e.g., VizWiz, POPE, SEED-I). No statistical significance or variance analysis is reported for these deltas.

A circularity concern is insufficiently addressed: the same data engine generates both GePBench and GePBench-train. The paper does not clearly establish that the evaluation split is independent of training data distribution beyond splitting easy/hard; even if images differ, the template-identical question distribution means LLaVA-GeP gains may reflect template fitting rather than transferable perception.

The synthetic-render setting limits ecological validity: Matplotlib line drawings with procedural noise differ substantially from the medical/fossil/downstream scenarios cited as motivation, and the observed anomaly that noise *improves* performance for several models (Appendix E.2) is acknowledged but not resolved, further weakening the claim that the benchmark measures robust real-world spatial perception.

Several analyses are cursory or internally inconsistent: the claim that higher resolution improves 'all aspects except location' is contradicted by Table 2 (Ref drops slightly, 42.5 -> 42.1); Appendix D says the LLM backbone is jointly finetuned while referencing a LoRA finetuning script; explanations for encoder behavior (positional embedding complexity) are speculative with no direct evidence.

Limited originality relative to concurrent work: perceptual-gap findings echo existing results (BLINK, 'Eyes Wide Shut', Cambrian-1), and the core novelty reduces to a template-driven synthetic dataset plus a fine-tuned LLaVA variant.
The limitations section is superficial, mentioning only model coverage and dataset size, and omitting the more substantive concerns above (synthetic-domain gap, distractor bias, train/eval overlap).

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely underexplored capability: foundational geometric perception of MLLMs, clearly distinguished from prior geometry-reasoning datasets (GeoQA, Geometry3K, GeoMM, MAVIS) which test higher-order mathematical reasoning.

The synthetic data engine is well designed and documented: structured textual descriptions guarantee ground-truth correctness by construction, avoid web-data contamination, and support controlled variations (noise, shape count, easy/hard splits).

The evaluation is broad (20 models including GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-1.5-Pro) and the comparison to OpenCompass scores plus the human-vs-model gap analysis (Figure 7) contextualizes the results nicely.
Useful ablations: number of shapes, visual encoder choice/resolution (Table 2), and noise effects (Figure 10), which yield actionable insights about positional embeddings and encoder design.

Reproducibility is addressed thoughtfully: exact checkpoints in Table 3, prompt template, answer-parsing scheme validated at 99.9%, human evaluation protocol, and training hyperparameters for LLaVA-GeP. Limitations are discussed honestly.
The downstream experiment (LLaVA-GeP) with a from-scratch LLaVA-1.5 control trained identically is a fair comparison design, demonstrating positive transfer to math/chart tasks.
weaknesses: Construct validity concerns: the benchmark uses Matplotlib-rendered synthetic figures, and the authors' own noise ablation (Figure 10) shows several models perform *better* on noisy figures, suggesting the clean synthetic distribution is out-of-distribution. It is therefore unclear how much of the observed failure reflects deficient geometric perception versus distribution mismatch with training data, weakening the central claim that the benchmark isolates a foundational perceptual deficit.

The size questions require numeric area estimation (e.g., 17.5% accuracy for GPT-4o). It is not established that distractor intervals are perceptually comparable across questions, and precise metric estimation may conflate perception with quantitative grounding; this should be analyzed rather than reported as a single 'perception' failure.

Multiple-choice evaluation risks known biases (answer-position bias, textual-only shortcuts). The paper does not report checks such as option shuffling consistency or text-only baselines for models like GPT-4o, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are provided for any comparison.

The downstream gains of LLaVA-GeP are modest (~2.2% average, with per-benchmark deltas of ~0.5-4 points) and presented without error bars; given evaluation noise, the conclusion that geometric perception data drives these improvements is suggestive rather than firmly established. Additionally, captions are generated by Qwen-2.5-14B, introducing a possible confound with the judge model used for evaluation (also Qwen-2.5-14B).
The scaling analysis ('limited improvements') relies on only a handful of model-size pairs from different model families, so it is anecdotal rather than a controlled scaling study.
Human evaluation involves only five undergraduates on sampled subsets, which is adequate but small; no inter-annotator agreement is reported.

Novelty is incremental relative to existing perceptual probes (BLINK, MMVP/Eyes Wide Shut) which already document that MLLMs 'see but do not perceive'; the main contribution is the geometry-specific instantiation and the data engine rather than a new finding.
